hints: Focus on what heating these gases can do, think about decomposition to hydrogen and the halogen vapour.
Recall the colours, bromine vapour is brown while iodine vapour is purple, and compare the H-Br and H-I bond strengths.
Ask which gas breaks apart first on heating, then check which tube can show colour while the other stays unchanged.
walkthrough:
**Write the possible decomposition reactions**

Heating can split the hydrogen halides into hydrogen and halogen. This is thermal decomposition.

$$2\text{HBr(g)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{(g)} + \text{Br}_2\text{(g) brown vapour}$$
$$2\text{HI(g)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{(g)} + \text{I}_2\text{(g) purple vapour}$$

**Compare thermal stability**

Stability falls down Group 17 because the H-X bond gets longer and weaker. The H-I bond is weaker than the H-Br bond, so HI needs less energy to break.

Bond strength: $\text{H-Br} > \text{H-I}$, so stability: $\text{HBr} > \text{HI}$.

**Decide what is possible at the same temperature**

At a low temperature, neither decomposes. At a middle temperature, only the weaker HI decomposes to give purple $\text{I}_2$. At a very high temperature, both decompose.

It is never possible for HBr to decompose while HI stays unchanged, because HI is always easier to break.

options.A: Incorrect. Brown vapour correctly identifies Br2 from HBr, but if HBr has enough energy to decompose, the weaker HI must also have decomposed. HI showing no change here is impossible.
options.B: Incorrect. HBr cannot give a purple vapour, purple is I2 not Br2. Also, HBr decomposing while HI shows no change is backwards, since HI is less stable than HBr.
options.C: Incorrect. It is true that HI can decompose while HBr stays unchanged, but the colour is wrong. Decomposition of HI gives purple I2 vapour, not brown Br2 vapour.
options.D: Correct. HI is thermally less stable than HBr, so on gentle heating HI alone decomposes to H2 and purple I2 vapour while HBr remains unchanged. This matches the bond strength trend perfectly.
